newsitem.title: FRANCE: Palestinian blasts Israel over water rights.
newsitem.headline: Palestinian blasts Israel over water rights.

text.p: The Palestinian delegate at a Euro-Mediterranean conference accused Israel on Tuesday of holding up progress on Palestinian water rights since the election of hardline Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"The Israelis want peace and also want to keep land -- and the water underneath -- but this cannot be achieved," Professor Riyad el-Khoudary said.

"Since the Israeli election, everything is being delayed. Either we are still under occupation or we are free from it," Khoudary said on the last day of the two-day conference of European Union, North African and Middle East states.
He added that a joint committee on water had not met since March and this delayed implementation of projects in the fledgling Palestinian economy. Netanyahu was elected in May.
Ram Aviram, Israel's director of multilateral peace talks cooordination, agreed water was an issue to be discussed in final settlement talks which have yet to start.

"But we have agreed between us on enough other frameworks where water can be raised and discussed. To the specific accusation that the joint water committee has not met since March, my information is that it has met twice in the last two months," Aviram told reporters.

Khoudary said on Monday that Israel was stealing water from Arab lands. "They are pumping our water from areas alongside the border with the result that about 30 percent of the water used in Israel comes from Arab sources -- mostly from Palestinian areas but also from Syria and Lebanon," he said.
Khoudary however told the conference that the Palestinian Authority was committed to the peace process "with our Israeli partners."
"If rights are agreed upon, this problem can be solved easily as long as Israel recognises our water rights," he said.
Delegates from both Israel and Syria attended the meeting, the first such joint appearance since Netanyahu's election.
The two countries have waged wars in the past over control of water resources and a common saying in the area is that the next Middle East war will not be over oil but over water.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette told the conference he hoped water would be a subject for cooperation after being one for confrontation in the same way France and Germany began their post-World War Two cooperation over steel and coal, long a bone of contention between them.
Attending the meeting were representatives of all 15 European Union countries and 12 North African and Middle East states.

Irish Secretary of State for the Environment Bernard Allen, representing the Irish presidency of the European Union, said demands on water resources were at unprecedented levels because of the intensification of agriculture, population growth and higher expectations on living standards and health.

The conference, which was told demand for water had doubled this century, adopted a series of recommendations including setting up a Euro-Mediterranean information system on water management ahead of setting up a Mediterranean Water Network.
Recommendations also included warnings of caution before liberalising agriculture in countries where it is often under close government control.
